observations.quote: CHAP. I. Of the True Physick.
observations.note: The chapter is headed and numbered as treating one thing, the True Physick.

observations.quote: THE true Physick whereof by the Devine assistance I intend here to treat
observations.note: The author announces in his own voice the thing he will treat here.

observations.quote: is the mear gift of the most high God
observations.note: The true Physick is said to be purely a gift of God.

observations.quote: it is not to be sought for or learned from the Heathens, but from God alone
observations.note: Physick is to be learned from God alone, not from the Heathens. The lines given do not say who the Heathens are. Margin note N036 names a writing of Paracels. at this point.

observations.quote: See Paracels. his Labyrinth of Physitians.
observations.name: Paracels. his Labyrinth of Physitians
observations.note: The margin sends the reader to a writing of Paracels., beside the statement that Physick is learned from God alone and not from the Heathens.

observations.quote: Wisdome therefore is not to be got from the Creatures, but from God, who being the first inventer of all Secrets, alone knoweth with what properties he hath indued every creature
observations.note: Wisdom comes from God, not from the Creatures; God, first inventer of all Secrets, alone knows the properties given to each creature.

observations.quote: no mortall Master or dead letter can ever teach it so well as he, who is the perfect Artist of all things
observations.note: No human master and no written letter teaches this as well as God, named the perfect Artist.

observations.quote: All learn of the first by retrogression or going backward, and this first of God, who gave him knowledge in his Creation
observations.note: The text glosses retrogression as going backward: all learn of the first, and the first learned of God at his creation. The lines given do not name who the first is.

observations.quote: A Physitian should be born out of the Light of Grace and Nature of the inward and invisible Man, the internall Angell, the Light of Nature, which like a sound Doctour teacheth and instructeth men
observations.note: The Physitian is to be born of the Light of Grace and Nature; the inward and invisible Man, the internall Angell and the Light of Nature stand side by side as the teacher of men, compared to the Holy Spirit teaching the Apostles.

observations.quote: It is perfected and brought to light by practice, not established by Humane, but by the institution of God and Nature
observations.note: It is perfected by practice and established by God and Nature, not by human institution.

observations.quote: upon Nature, upon which God hath written with his own sacred finger in sublunary things, but especially in perfect Mettalls
observations.note: Physick is founded on Nature, spoken of as a writing by God's finger in sublunary things; perfect Mettalls are marked as the chief place of that writing.

observations.quote: God therefore is the true Foundation thereof
observations.note: God is named the true Foundation of Physick.

observations.quote: The Master teacheth that Scholler in vaine whose Nativity is not disposed to that Art by the Sears.
observations.note: The margin says teaching is in vain for a scholar whose Nativity is not disposed to the Art. The last word is printed Sears; the lines given do not explain it.

observations.quote: Physick is nothing else but the created and incarnate Mercy of our Heavenly Father, bestowed upon poor afflicted Mortalls
observations.note: The text says what Physick is: the created and incarnate Mercy of God, given to afflicted mortals, so that God is glorified.

observations.quote: that the sick Patient might sensibly perceive and have experience of the bountifull love, mercifulnesse and assistance of his Creator towards him in his afflictions
observations.note: The purpose of Physick: that the sick may perceive by the senses the love and help of the Creator.

observations.quote: Physick is a favour given of God, whereof University books are not the Foundation, but the invisible mercy of God and his speciall gift
observations.note: The margin denies that University books are the foundation of Physick and sets God's mercy and gift in their place.

observations.quote: This Physicall essence in Phisick is called Gold.
observations.note: The margin gives the name Gold to this Physicall essence in Phisick; the word names an essence, not plainly the metal. The note does not say further what the essence is.

observations.quote: Physick is written in the book of Nature (1) in Heaven and Earth, and may there be read & found out by Chyromancy and phisiognomy
observations.note: Physick is spoken of as written in the book of Nature, in Heaven and Earth, and read there by Chyromancy and phisiognomy through the miraculous illumination of God.

observations.quote: this Medicine, as naturall Mummy and kernell of Nature, is contained in the vitall Sulphur, as in the treasure of Nature
observations.note: The Medicine is called naturall Mummy and kernell of Nature, and is placed in the vitall Sulphur.

observations.quote: is founded in the Balsam of Vegetables, Mineralls and Animalls, from which every action in Nature hath its beginning
observations.note: The Medicine is founded in a Balsam present in all three kinds, the beginning of every action in Nature.

observations.quote: By its onely power all diseases are cured
observations.note: This Medicine alone is said to cure all diseases, on the condition that follows.

observations.quote: if (as shall be shewed anon) it be rightly prepared
observations.note: The author promises to show later how the Medicine is rightly prepared.

observations.quote: it be rightly prepared, and separated from all impurity, and in a due order conveniently administred by a Godly skilfull Phisitian to the poor, weak, decayed Nature of Man
observations.note: Steps named as the condition of the cure: preparing, separating from all impurity, administering in due order by a godly skilful Phisitian. How each is done is not given in these lines.

observations.quote: The Foundation of this Physick is according to the agreement of the lesser World Man with the greater and externall world
observations.note: The foundation of Physick is the agreement of Man, the lesser World, with the greater outer world.

observations.quote: Astronomy and Philosophy, which explaine those two Globes, the superiour and inferiour
observations.what: those two Globes, the superiour and inferiour
observations.note: Two Globes, an upper and a lower, are set apart, each explained by one study.

observations.quote: Philosophy teatheth the force and properties of Earth and Wate,-as Astronomy doth of the Firmament and Aire
observations.note: The text says what each word covers here: Philosophy the force and properties of Earth and Water, Astronomy those of Firmament and Aire.

observations.quote: Phylosophy and Astronomy make up an internall and perfect Phylosopher, not onely in the great World, but also in the lesser
observations.note: The two studies together make the perfect Phylosopher, in the great World and in the lesser.

observations.quote: it is necessary to accommodate the disposition of the great World as of a parent to the little World as to the Son, and duly compare the Anotomy of the World with the Anotomy of Man
observations.note: The method required: fit the great World as parent to the little World as son, and compare the Anotomy of the one with that of the other.

observations.quote: The outward World is a speculative Anotomy, wherein we may see, as in a glasse, the lesser World Man
observations.note: The outward World is said to be a speculative Anotomy, a glass in which Man is seen.

observations.quote: so much of his wonderfull and excellent fabrick and creation as is necessary for a Physitian to know, cannot be understood from the man himselfe
observations.note: What a Physitian must know of Man cannot be learned from the man himself.

observations.quote: What the Light of Nature is.
observations.note: The margin heads the passage as saying what the Light of Nature is.

observations.quote: but in all their powers and vertues; as is the great world, so is the lesser, in essence and internall form they are altogether one and the same thing
observations.note: Great and lesser world agree not in outward form but in all powers and vertues; in essence and internall form they are one and the same.

observations.quote: Without the knowledge of Light of Nature or the great world no Physitian can have an exact knowledge of diseases in Man.
observations.note: Knowledge of the Light of Nature, or the great world, is made the condition of knowing diseases in Man; the or sets the two side by side.

observations.quote: the Light of Nature, which is nothing else but a divine Analogy of this visible world with the body of man
observations.note: The text says what the Light of Nature is: a divine Analogy of the visible world with the body of man.

observations.quote: whatsoever lyeth hid and unseen in Man, is made manifest in the visible Anotomy of the whole Universe, for the Microcosmicall Nature in Man is invisible and incomprehensible
observations.note: What lies hid in Man is made manifest in the visible Universe, because the Microcosmicall Nature in Man is invisible. The hiding is in Man, not a withholding by the writer.

observations.quote: The great World is a speculation and glasse of the little World Man.
observations.note: The margin restates that the great World is the glass of Man.

observations.quote: Heaven and Earth are Man's Parents, out of which Man last of all was created
observations.note: Heaven and Earth are called Man's Parents; Man was created last, out of them.

observations.quote: and can Anotomize them, hath attained the true knowledge of their child Man, the most perfect creature in all his properties
observations.note: Whoever knows and can Anotomize the parents, Heaven and Earth, has the true knowledge of Man.

observations.quote: Man is the End of Phylosophy and Astronomy.
observations.note: The margin names Man as the End of the two studies.

observations.quote: all things of the whole Universe meet in him as in the Centre, and the Anotomy of him in his Nature is the Anotomy of the whole world
observations.note: All things meet in Man as in the Centre; his Anotomy is that of the whole world.

observations.quote: The externall world is the figure of Man, and Man is an hidden world, because visible things in him are invisible, and when they are made visible then they are diseases, not health
observations.note: Man is called an hidden world, with the reason given: visible things in him are invisible, and when they are made visible in him they are diseases, not health.

observations.quote: this is the true knowledge, that Man may Microcosmically be known visibly and invisibly or magically
observations.note: invisibly or magically sets the two words side by side, so that magically here seems to name the invisible way of knowing Man. This rests on the one word or.

observations.quote: The knowledge of every sound and perfect Physitian proceedeth from the true and full Anotomy both of the great and little world
observations.note: The Physitian's knowledge comes from the Anotomy of both worlds.

observations.quote: the Nature, as well of the Macrocosme as the Microcosme, is its own medicine, disease, and Physitian
observations.note: Nature, in the great world and in the little, is its own medicine, disease and Physitian.

observations.quote: Nature, not man, maketh a Physitian.
observations.note: A Physitian is made by Nature, not by man.

observations.quote: the Matter of Man is the Extract of the four Elements
observations.note: The matter of Man is the Extract of the four Elements, so he must be familiar with them and their fruits.

observations.quote: God created the Elements for their fruits sake, that they might sustaine and preserve Man with food and Physick.
observations.note: The Elements were created for their fruits, which give Man food and Physick.

observations.quote: The knowledge of the 4 Elements doe shew every disease in man and its cure.
observations.note: The margin says knowledge of the four Elements shows every disease and its cure.

observations.quote: all the externall Elements represent unto us the whole Man, which being known, Man also is understood, for they are alike, and are the very Microcosm
observations.note: The outer Elements represent the whole Man; knowing them, Man is understood.

observations.quote: in the foure Elements there is but one Anatomy essence and matter, all the differenc being onely in the Form
observations.note: The four Elements are one in Anatomy, essence and matter and differ only in Form.

observations.quote: The knowledge of Physick in the outward world is to be fetched from the Limbovn, and depends upon the knowledg of Man.
observations.note: The margin sends knowledge of Physick in the outer world to the Limbovn, a word spelled so in the text given and not explained in these lines.

observations.quote: Thus in all things there is Fire, Aire, Earthy Water.
observations.note: A series of mixed elements is set out in four steps (Thus, Againe, Likewise, Lastly), each Element named with the qualities of others; as printed the series is irregular and does not give four full sets.

observations.quote: There are also four kinds of Mercury, and four sorts of Mettalls, a fourfold Snow, four sorts of Ametheists and precious stones
observations.what: four kinds of Mercury, and four sorts of Mettalls
observations.note: Mercury, Mettalls, Snow and stones are each counted as four kinds.

observations.quote: There are Foure of every thing, one in the Firmament or Heavenly Element
observations.note: Every thing is four, one each in Firmament, Aire, Water and Earth. The Firmament is here called the Heavenly Element.

observations.quote: Every Element perfecteth its power and operation in all the four Elements.
observations.note: The margin says each Element works out its power in all four.

observations.quote: So there is a fourfold Man
observations.note: Man too is named fourfold. The lines given do not list the four.

observations.quote: God is far more wonderfull in his invisible works then in his visible
observations.note: God's invisible works are set above his visible ones.

observations.quote: Paracelsus faith, that to avoyd an Emptiness in all the four Elements, he created living creatures
observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.note: The account of the inhabitants of the Elements is given as what Paracelsus says (the verb is printed faith). The lines do not name who he is. CH1.8 to CH1.11 appear to continue it; the text does not mark where his words end.

observations.quote: inanimate, that is to say, without an Intellectuall Soule
observations.note: The text says what inanimate means here: without an Intellectuall Soule, said of creatures that are living.

observations.quote: which should be the four kind of Inhabitants of the Elements, who differ from Men created after the Image of God, in understanding, wisdome, arts, operations, and habitations
observations.what: the four kind of Inhabitants of the Elements
observations.note: Four kinds of Inhabitants of the Elements are set apart from Men made after the Image of God.

observations.quote: To the Water there belong Nimphs, Undens, Melosyns, whose Monsters or bastards are the Syrens that swim upon the water.
observations.note: The inhabitants of Water and their Monsters are named. The paragraph follows the report of Paracelsus; it does not itself say whose words it is.

observations.quote: To the Earth doe belong Gnoms, Lemurs, Sylphs, Montans, Zonnets, whose Monsters are the Pigmyes.
observations.what: Gnoms, Lemurs, Sylphs, Montans, Zonnets; Pigmyes
observations.note: The inhabitants of Earth and their Monsters are named; Sylphs stand here under Earth.

observations.quote: Satyrs, whose Monsters are the Gyants
observations.note: The inhabitants of the Aire, called our airy world, and their Monsters, the Gyants, are named; one name in the list has an illegible letter.

observations.quote: To the Fire or the Firmament doe belong the Vulcanals, Pennats, Salamanders, Superi, whose Monsters are Zundell
observations.note: The inhabitants of Fire and their Monsters are named. Fire and Firmament are joined by or as one Element.

observations.quote: Flagae which Theophrastus in his works affirmeth are in many thousands of severall forts incorporated to the Soul of the World
observations.name: Theophrastus
observations.note: The Flagae, in many thousands, incorporated to the Soul of the World, are reported as what Theophrastus affirms in his works.

observations.quote: Thus also there is a fourfold Medicine
observations.note: Medicine is named fourfold, matching the fourfold Elements and Man.

observations.quote: the fiery, airy, watry, earthy Heart of the Macrocosm in all things agreeable to the Heart of the Microcosm Man
observations.note: The example of the fourfold Medicine: a Heart of the Macrocosm in four kinds agrees with the Heart of Man.

observations.quote: the Microcosm the child ought always to answer to the fourfold members of the Macrocosm its parent
observations.note: Each member of Man answers to fourfold members of the great world.

observations.quote: every malady and medicine is of the same Physiognomy, Chyromancy and Anotomy; He that knows not this Fundamentall cannot be a good Phisitian
observations.note: Disease and medicine share one Physiognomy, Chyromancy and Anotomy; this is named a Fundamentall without which no one is a good Phisitian.

observations.quote: we find out of ancient Records that Astrologers and Chymiologers were very near of kin
observations.name: ancient Records
observations.note: On the authority of ancient Records, not named further, Astrologers and Chymiologers are said to be near of kin.

observations.quote: both have their own Heaven, their own Sun, their own Moon, their Planets, and their own proper Stars
observations.note: The lower astronomy is said to have its own Heaven, Sun, Moon, Planets and Stars; these words are used here also of things other than those of the sky.

observations.quote: the Astrology of superiour things hath to doe with the Chymiology of things inferiour
observations.note: Astrology of things above and Chymiology of things below belong together.

observations.quote: Those Chymists who by the assistance of divine Grace have attained the Mind
observations.note: The Mind is used as the name of something attained by divine Grace, the condition for fitting the upper bodies to the lower and unfolding the enigmas; the understanding is tied to some only. The lines given do not say what the Mind is.

observations.quote: these can easily and truly unfold all Phylosophicall difficulties that have been wrapt up in aenigmaticall obscurity
observations.note: Philosophical matters are said to have been wrapt up in aenigmaticall obscurity; only such Chymists can unfold them.

observations.quote: they need not travell to India or America to get the knowledge of Phylosophy
observations.note: Given as what such Chymists will confesse: no journey to far lands is needed for Phylosophy.

observations.quote: the invisible Astra's of the other Elements should be represented by a visible appearance in the supream Element
observations.note: The other Elements have invisible Astra's; these are shown visibly in the highest Element.

observations.quote: there be nothing in the whole course of the inferiour Nature which by the in-bred Astra's is not able to justifie the lawfull use of Astronomy
observations.note: Lower Nature has in-bred Astra's of its own, which justify the use of Astronomy there.

observations.quote: Thus as P. Severinus the Dane doth learnedly observe
observations.name: P. Severinus the Dane
observations.note: The account of the constellations of the seasons contained in Earth, Water and Aire is given as Severinus's observation.

observations.quote: the (Sidus) constellation of Summer, Winter, Spring Autumn, are contained in the Earth, Water, Aire
observations.note: The word Sidus stands in brackets beside constellation as its gloss.

observations.quote: to which onely many of the common Phylosophers by a great mistake have ascribed all Astronomy
observations.name: common Phylosophers
observations.note: A view of the common Phylosophers is reported in order to reject it: that all Astronomy belongs to the Astra's of the Firmament only.

observations.quote: we should blame the impressions of the Heavenly (Astra's) as barren in the time of dearth
observations.note: Within the observation given to Severinus: unless the constellations in the lower Elements worked together with those of the Firmament, dearth would be laid to the heavenly ones.

observations.quote: In his Idaea of Phylosophical Phifick.
observations.name: Idaea of Phylosophical Phifick
observations.note: The margin names the writing of Severinus from which the observation in CH1.13 is taken.

observations.quote: They that are troubled with the gout have a foresence of the sudden change of seasons
observations.note: The margin's example: the gouty feel the change of seasons beforehand; their pain makes them Prophets and Astrologers against their will.

observations.quote: The Internall Elements of man have a foresence of the change of Externall.
observations.note: The margin says the inner Elements of man feel beforehand the change of the outer.

observations.quote: As Reason rules the outward Astra's, so Physick rules the inward.
observations.note: The margin sets two rules side by side: Reason over the outward Astra's, Physick over the inward.

observations.quote: The Astrum of Man and Heaven is but one.
observations.note: The margin says the Astrum of Man and of Heaven is one.

observations.quote: There is a twofold Heaven
observations.note: Heaven is named twofold, Externall and Internall.

observations.quote: Internall, which is the Astrum or invisible and insensible body in all the Stars of Heaven
observations.note: The Internall Heaven is said to be the Astrum, an invisible and insensible body in all the Stars; the Externall is the bodies of the Astra's in the Firmament.

observations.quote: That invisible and insensible body of the Astra's is the Spirit of the World, or Nature
observations.note: The invisible body of the Astra's is said to be the Spirit of the World, or Nature; the name Hylech that follows is given as Paracelsus's.

observations.quote: as Paracelsus calls it, the Hylech
observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.note: The name Hylech is given as Paracelsus's word.

observations.quote: the internall Heaven of Man, which is the Olimpick spirit, doth particularly comprehend all the Astra's
observations.note: The inner Heaven of Man is said to be the Olimpick spirit, holding all the Astra's as the Hylech does in the great World.

observations.quote: the invisible Man is not onely all the Astra's, but is altogether one and the same thing with the Spirit of the world, as whitenesse is with snow
observations.note: The invisible Man is one and the same with the Spirit of the world.

observations.quote: As all things spring and proceed from within, from (things) hidden and invisible; so also the visible corporall substances proceed from incorporall, spirituall (things) out of the Astra's, and are the bodies of the Astra's
observations.note: Visible bodies come from hidden, invisible, spiritual things, out of the Astra's, are the bodies of the Astra's and remain in them.

observations.quote: are indued with a syderiall spirit, which is called Heaven or the Astrum, the secret Forger, from which every Formation, Figure and Colour of things proceedeth
observations.note: All things, stones and mettalls included, have a syderiall spirit, called Heaven, the Astrum, the secret Forger; form, figure and colour come from it.

observations.quote: this proper and internall Astrum, viz. The Sun of the Microcosm
observations.note: Man's own inner Astrum is named the Sun of the Microcosm; Sun is here said of something within Man. The name Ens that follows, glossed Being, is given as Paracelsus's.

observations.quote: which Paracelsus calls the Ens or Being of the seed and virtue or power
observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.note: The name Ens for the inner Astrum is given as Paracelsus's. From it Man is said to be generated, formed and governed.

observations.quote: as iron in the imagination of the Smith
observations.note: The margin likens the forming of things in the Astra to iron in the imagination of the Smith.

observations.quote: Hence also Nativities are to be cast
observations.note: The margin draws from the forming power of the Astra that Nativities are to be cast.

observations.quote: in Paramiro de eme Astro
observations.name: Paramiro
observations.note: The margin sends the reader to a writing, Paramiro; the author's name before it and the last word of the title each have an illegible letter.

observations.quote: it is not meant of the visible coales of Heaven, nor of the invisible body of the Astra's in the Firmament, but of every things own proper Astrum
observations.note: The text says what its own phrase means: the astra's from which all form proceeds are neither the visible stars nor their invisible body in the Firmament, but each thing's own Astrum.

observations.quote: the superior doth not power forth its vertues & hidden secrets into the inferiour spectificate Firmament
observations.note: The superior heaven does not pour its vertues and hidden secrets into lower things.

observations.quote: nor of the invisible body of the Astra's in the Firmament, but of every things own proper Astrum
observations.note: Here form does not proceed from the invisible body of the Astra's in the Firmament; in CH1.14 that invisible body is the Spirit of the World and the invisible Man is one and the same thing with it, and N046 says the Astrum of Man and Heaven is but one. The text given does not settle how they agree.

observations.quote: as the false Philosophers thinke that the stars of the Firmament do infuse virtue into herbs and trees
observations.name: false Philosophers
observations.note: A view reported in order to reject it (no in no wise).

observations.quote: every growing and living thing carry its proper heaven and Astrum with it selfe, and in it selfe
observations.note: Each growing and living thing has its own heaven and Astrum within it.

observations.quote: the superiour stars in their course through the Zodiak excite and stir up the growth of inferiour things, they provide for them by dew raine, seasons, but do not infuse the internall Astrum into things that grow
observations.note: The upper stars only stir up growth and provide dew, rain and seasons; they do not give the inner Astrum, smell, colour or form.

observations.quote: all things proceed from the inner Astrum or secret forger, and not from without
observations.note: Smell, colour and form come from the inner Astrum, again called secret forger.

observations.quote: the externall stars do neither incline nor necessitate Man
observations.note: The outer stars neither incline nor compel Man.

observations.quote: but Man rather inclines the Stars, and by his Magicall imagination infecteth them, and causeth those deadly impressions
observations.note: Man inclines the Stars and by his Magicall imagination infects them and causes deadly impressions.

observations.quote: Man governeth the Stars and not the Stars him.
observations.note: The margin restates that Man governs the Stars.

observations.quote: we receive not our conditions, properties, and manners from the Ascendant, nor from the Constellation of the Planets, but from the hand of God through the breathing in of the breath of life
observations.note: Man's conditions and manners come from God by the breath of life, not from the Ascendant or the Planets. Margin note N049 names the eight Psalme at the end of these words.

observations.quote: the externall stars do neither incline nor necessitate Man
observations.note: Here the stars neither incline Man and his conditions do not come from the Ascendant or Planets; N037 speaks of a scholar's Nativity disposed to an Art, and N047 says Nativities are to be cast. N047 speaks of the Astra in which things are formed, which CH1.16 says are each thing's own; the lines given do not settle it.

observations.quote: Read the eight Psalme.
observations.name: the eight Psalme
observations.note: The margin sends the reader to a Psalm beside the words on the breath of life and Man's rule over the Stars.

observations.quote: So that Mans Reason ought to rule the externall Stars.
observations.note: Man's Reason ought to rule the outer Stars.

observations.quote: if we that are the children of Adam did not provoke our Father with our sins we should alwayes find him meek and gentle towards us
observations.note: Harm is laid to our sins provoking our Father, not to the stars. The lines given do not say who our Father is here. A reference to Paracels. follows these words in the text and in N050.

observations.quote: see Paracels. in Paramiro lib. 2. de origine morbor. cap. 7.
observations.name: Paracels. in Paramiro
observations.note: The text sends the reader to a named book and chapter of Paracels. for the foregoing.

observations.quote: Vid. Paracels.
observations.name: Paracels.
observations.note: The margin names Paracels. beside the same sentence.

observations.quote: The course of the externall Firmament is free with its constellations, and is governed by none
observations.note: The outer Firmament runs free and is governed by none.

observations.quote: is governed by none
observations.note: Here the outer Firmament is governed by none; CH1.16 says Man inclines the Stars and his Reason ought to rule them, N048 that Man governs the Stars, N046 that Reason rules the outward Astra's.

observations.quote: the course of the Firmament and Stars in Man is free, with their Constellations, and not at all governed by the outward Firmament, which course is not finished materially, but in the spirits of bodies
observations.note: Man has a Firmament and Stars within, free of the outer one as the outer is free of all; their course is run in the spirits of bodies, not materially.

observations.quote: its own internall Astrum, or inward Heaven, from the Centre to the Circumference
observations.note: The inner Astrum is called the inward Heaven; fruit grows out of it from the centre outwards and is not set on the tree by Aire or Sun.

observations.quote: much lesse can the externall superiour Heaven infuse any vertue into the things that grow
observations.note: As the Aire or Sun cannot set an apple or pear upon the tree, much less does the outer Heaven give virtue to growing things.

observations.quote: the fruits of those Astra's or Caelestiall, Ayry, Earthy, Watry seeds doe indeavour and bend to one generall Good as Citizens of the same Anotmy
observations.note: The Astra's are here also called seeds of four kinds; their fruits serve one common good and help one another.

observations.quote: This visible and invisible fellowship of Nature is that golden chaine so much commended, this is the marriage of heaven and riches, these are Plato's rings
observations.note: The text says what three names mean: the golden chaine, the marriage of heaven and riches and Plato's rings are the fellowship of Nature just described.

observations.quote: Plato's Rings and Homers Chaines are nothing but a Divine Series and Order serving Providence, a graduall and concatenate Sympathy of things.
observations.note: The margin says what the two names mean: an order serving Providence, a linked Sympathy of things. It names Homer for the chains, which the paragraph leaves unnamed.

observations.quote: this is that dark and close Phylosophy so hard to be known in the most inward and secret parts of Natare
observations.note: This fellowship is called a dark and close Phylosophy, hard to know, lying in the inward and secret parts of Nature.

observations.quote: Democritus, Pythagoras, Plato, Apollonius, &c. have travelled to the Brachmans and Gymnosophists in the Indies, and to Hermes his Pillars in Aegypt
observations.note: Named persons are said to have travelled to the Indies and Aegypt to gain this Phylosophy; CH1.12 says Chymists who have attained the Mind need not travel to India or America.

observations.quote: This was that which the most ancient Phylosophers studied, which by the Light of Nature that singular inspiration of God they also obtained
observations.note: The most ancient Phylosophers obtained it by the Light of Nature, here called a singular inspiration of God.

observations.quote: the Light of Nature that singular inspiration of God
observations.note: CH1.5 says the Light of Nature is nothing else but a divine Analogy of the visible world with the body of man; here it is an inspiration of God, and CH1.1 sets it beside the inward Man and internall Angell. Three sayings that do not plainly agree.

observations.quote: there are THREE Principles of all things which are found in every compound body
observations.note: Three Principles are announced, the word THREE in capitals, found in every compound body.

observations.quote: No body compos'd by Nature can by any dissolving skill be parted into more or lesse then Three, viz. Into Mercury or liquor, Sulphur or Oyle, and Salt
observations.note: No natural body can be parted by any dissolving skill into more or fewer than three: Mercury or liquor, Sulphur or Oyle, Salt.

observations.quote: Mercury or liquor, Sulphur or Oyle, and Salt
observations.note: Two of the three are given a second name each: Mercury is liquor, Sulphur is Oyle.

observations.quote: the Holy Triunity when it spake that Triune word FIAT created all things Triune, as in a Spagiricall resolution is plainly to be seen
observations.note: All things were created threefold by the Triune word FIAT; this is said to be plainly seen in a Spagiricall resolution.

observations.quote: i. e. A seperation of purity from impurity, or truth from falshood.
observations.note: The margin says what the Spagiricall resolution is: a separation of purity from impurity, or truth from falshood; the second half gives the word a sense beyond the handling of bodies.

observations.quote: By the word FIAT (or Let there be) God produced the first matter, which is threefold in respect of the three Principles contained in the first
observations.note: FIAT is glossed Let there be; the first matter is said to be threefold, holding the three Principles.

observations.quote: afterward these three Species are seperated into four divers bodies, or Elements
observations.note: The three are afterwards separated into four bodies, the Elements.

observations.quote: a skillfull Artist should out of lead make red lead, white lead, Glasse, and the Spirit of lead
observations.note: A piece of work given as a likeness of the first matter separated into four Elements: from lead an Artist makes red lead, white lead, Glasse and the Spirit of lead. How is not said.

observations.quote: the world with all created bodies in it is nothing else but a fume or smoak coagulated or curded together of the three substances, Sulphur Salt, Mercury
observations.note: The world and all bodies are said to be nothing else but a fume or smoak coagulated of the three substances.

observations.quote: The Spagyricks can make this plaine by visible experience and uncontroulable certainty.
observations.note: The author appeals to the Spagyricks, who can show the three by visible experience.

observations.quote: the first watry like fugitive Mercury or Quicksilver; which preserveth the wood from burning
observations.note: In green wood the first moisture is watery, likened to fugitive Mercury or Quicksilver, and keeps the wood from burning.

observations.quote: these two are consumed by the fire; The third, viz. the Salt is unctuous, very little, thin and lasting, and remains in the ashes
observations.note: Burning green wood: the watery moisture like Mercury and the oily one like brimstone are consumed by the fire; the third, the Salt, remains in the ashes.

observations.quote: the Earth as it is indued with that threefold substance of Salt, Mercury and Sulphur, is the cause of the materiall body of man
observations.note: The Earth, having the three substances, is cause of man's material body. CH1.6 calls the Matter of Man the Extract of the four Elements.

observations.quote: The Salt by coagulation gives Solidity, Colour and Tast to all bodies
observations.note: What the Salt does in bodies: by coagulation it gives solidity, colour and taste.

observations.quote: The Sulphur by a pleasant mixture tempereth the coagulation of the Salt, and gives the Body Substance and Transmutation
observations.note: What the Sulphur does: tempers the Salt's coagulation and gives substance and Transmutation.

observations.quote: Mercury, which like the Elixir giveth the vertues
observations.note: Mercury gives the virtues, operations and secrets and is likened to the Elixir, which these lines do not explain.

observations.quote: by a diligent and constant supply of the vital and vegetative moysture doth cherish the two former, which by frequent action continually grow dry and old
observations.note: Mercury feeds the other two with moisture, as they grow dry and old by action.

observations.quote: When the Salt or Mummy is spent things
observations.note: The margin joins Salt and Mummy by or as one thing that can be spent; the word after has illegible letters. CH1.3 called the Medicine naturall Mummy contained in the vitall Sulphur.

observations.quote: These three Principles which are in all bodies are altogether distinct in use and properties by reason of the mixture of the vertue or operation, although to sence they present but one simular substance of bodies
observations.note: The three Principles differ in use and properties, though to the senses a body shows one like substance.

observations.quote: Some Theophrastaeans, who have more narrowly and exactly searched out the causes of hidden things doe add a Fourth
observations.name: Some Theophrastaeans
observations.note: A fourth Principle is reported as added by Some Theophrastaeans, said to have searched hidden things more exactly; not given as the author's own.

observations.quote: which they call the Spirit, which though it may be got out of Mineralls and Vegetables
observations.note: The fourth is what the Theophrastaeans call the Spirit; it can be got out of Mineralls and Vegetables but not out of Animalls, by reason of its subtility.

observations.quote: nor can it be extracted or seperated by the skill of Art, and therefore cannot be had
observations.note: A limit of the work, in the Theophrastaeans' report: in Animalls the Spirit cannot be extracted or separated by Art.

observations.quote: thus Sulphur or brimstone may answer to Fire, Salt to the earth, Mercury to Water, Spirit to Aire
observations.note: The four are set against the four Elements, one to one; Sulphur is also called brimstone.

observations.quote: doe add a Fourth
observations.note: CH1.19 says no natural body can be parted into more or fewer than Three; here a Fourth is added, in the name of Some Theophrastaeans, and the author does not reject it in these lines.

observations.quote: The Spirit of God upon the face of the waters.
observations.note: The margin sets the Spirit of God beside the fourth Principle called the Spirit. The note does not say how the two belong together.

observations.quote: seeing we have entred into a Discourse of the Elements
observations.note: The author names what he is now in as a Discourse of the Elements.

observations.quote: we shall add a few things concerning them out of that short Treatise of Severinus
observations.name: Severinus
observations.note: What follows on the Elements is announced as taken out of a short Treatise of Severinus; the lines given do not mark where the borrowing ends.

observations.quote: The true and purely spirituall Elements are the keepers, nurses, places, Mines, wombs and receptacles of the whole Creation; yea the very essence, existence, life and act of all Beings
observations.note: What the true Elements are, in the part announced as from Severinus: spiritual keepers, places and wombs of the Creation, and the life and act of all Beings.

observations.quote: Places are not without Things, but are filled with their properties, which administer life and nourishment to the things that are in them
observations.note: The Elements as places are filled with properties that feed what is in them.

observations.quote: to the Seeds that they may produce out of themselves the things that were secretly treasured up in them
observations.note: The Seeds hold things secretly treasured up in them, which they bring forth. A hiding in things, not by the writer.

observations.quote: These (places) are divided into two Globes, viz. the superiour Fire, or the Firmament, and Aire, much like the shell and white of an egge; the inferiour, Water and the Earth, like the yolk of an egge
observations.note: The Elements are divided into two Globes and likened to an egg: Fire or Firmament and Aire the shell and white, Water and Earth the yolk. CH1.4 names two Globes, the superiour and inferiour.

observations.quote: In these four incorporeall, empty, voyd Natures, the Creatour by vertue of the Word opening the united multitude
observations.note: The four Elements are called incorporeall, empty, voyd Natures in which the Creatour works by the Word. Whether these are still words out of Severinus the lines do not show.

observations.quote: Gen. 1.
observations.name: Gen. 1.
observations.note: The margin names Gen. 1. beside the words on the Word and the Spirit upon the Waters.

observations.quote: and of the Spirit moving upon the face of the Waters, did plant the Light and Seminall causes of all things
observations.note: By the Word and the Spirit the Creatour planted in the four Natures the Light and the Seminall causes of all things.

observations.quote: shall ever be supplyed by an incomprehensible Magick out of the Eternall Treasures of Divine Wisdome
observations.note: The ongoing supply of what was planted in the Elements is called an incomprehensible Magick out of Divine Wisdome.

observations.quote: knitting the Principles of bodies together wherewith they might be covered as with a house or garment, and which are to last as long as this worldly frame
observations.note: The Principles of bodies are knit together as a house or garment that covers what was planted.

observations.quote: The Seeds and Astra's, those bonds of things, lay hid in the invisible Treasures of the Elements from the beginning of the Creation, as in a great deep
observations.note: The Seeds and Astra's, called bonds of things, lay hid in the Elements from the Creation and spring up at their appointed times. A hiding in Nature, not by the writer.

observations.quote: by their help the World is governed, indeavoring to imitate Eternity by a continuall addition of fresh supply
observations.note: By the Seeds and Astra's the Elements agree and the World is governed.

observations.quote: The knowledge of the Elements cannot be attained unto without these Seeds, because they declare or open the use and services of the Elements
observations.note: The Elements cannot be known without the Seeds, which open their use.

observations.quote: as the seeds are to the Elements, so the Principles of bodies are to them; which Principles being the inseperable companions of the Seeds, cleaves to them as intermingled by an indissoluble tye
observations.note: A proportion is stated between Seeds, Elements and Principles of bodies; the Principles cling to the Seeds by an indissoluble tye.

observations.quote: the Seeds and Principles of Things receive strength of Generation and Multiplication from the authority of His Word, whose command all things obey
observations.note: Seeds and Principles have their power to generate and multiply from the Word.

observations.quote: Hippocr. in lib. de Antiqua medic.
observations.name: Hippocr. in lib. de Antiqua medic.
observations.note: The margin names a writing of Hippocr. beside the passage.

observations.quote: But as the Seeds and Elements can hardly be seperated one from the other by the sharpest wit
observations.note: Seeds and Elements can hardly be told apart even by the sharpest wit.

observations.quote: All things proceeds from their powers.
observations.note: The margin says all things proceed from their powers; the note does not say whose.

observations.quote: so neither can the Elements and Principles of bodies, the lawes of Nature scarce ever suffered them perfectly to be seperated by any industry of Art
observations.note: A limit of the work: Elements and Principles of bodies are scarce ever perfectly separated by Art.

observations.quote: the lawes of Nature scarce ever suffered them perfectly to be seperated by any industry of Art
observations.note: Here Elements and Principles are scarce ever perfectly separated by Art; CH1.19 says bodies are parted into the three by dissolving skill, plainly seen in a Spagiricall resolution and made plain by the Spagyricks. The two may speak of different separations, and CH1.23 may still be Severinus's matter; the text given does not settle it.

dropped.reason: CH1.12 calls the Caelestiall Astronomy parent of the inferior astronomy, a relation of studies; it says nothing of heaven infusing virtue, so the two passages do not meet as a conflict.

voices.quote: it is not to be sought for or learned from the Heathens
voices.basis: Margin note N036 'See Paracels. his Labyrinth of Physitians' stands at the end of these words; the text does not say whether they are his.

voices.quote: Paracelsus faith, that to avoyd an Emptiness
voices.basis: Named, with the verb printed faith and a report introduced by that.
The lists of inhabitants follow the report given to Paracelsus in CH1.7 with no new speaker; the text does not mark where his words end.

voices.quote: Flagae which Theophrastus in his works affirmeth
voices.basis: Named, with the verb affirmeth and in his works.

voices.quote: Astrologers and Chymiologers were very near of kin
voices.basis: we find out of ancient Records that.

voices.quote: henceforth they need not travell to India or America
voices.basis: Given as what those Chymists will confesse.

voices.quote: Thus as P. Severinus the Dane doth learnedly observe
voices.basis: Named with the verb observe; margin note N046 names his Idaea of Phylosophical Phifick.

voices.quote: to which onely many of the common Phylosophers
voices.basis: Their view is reported as ascribed by a great mistake, to be rejected.

voices.quote: as Paracelsus calls it, the Hylech
voices.basis: Named with the verb calls; covers the name only.
Named with the verb calls; covers the name only.
Their view is reported with the verb thinke and rejected (no in no wise).

voices.quote: For we receive not our conditions
voices.basis: Margin note N049 'Read the eight Psalme.' stands at the end of these words; the text does not say whether they are drawn from it.

voices.quote: For if we that are the children of Adam
voices.basis: The text's 'see Paracels. in Paramiro lib. 2.' and margin note N050 'Vid. Paracels.' follow these words; the text does not say whether they are his.

voices.quote: Some Theophrastaeans, who have more narrowly
voices.basis: Their addition of a Fourth is reported (doe add, which they call); the rest of the paragraph describes that Fourth and sets the four against the Elements, with no other speaker marked.

voices.quote: The true and purely spirituall Elements
voices.basis: Announced: we shall add a few things concerning them out of that short Treatise of Severinus.

voices.quote: In these four incorporeall, empty, voyd Natures
voices.basis: Continues the matter announced from Severinus; the text does not mark where it ends. Margin notes N055 'Gen. 1.' and N056 'Hippocr. in lib. de Antiqua medic.' name writings beside its words.
